title: Jonah and Daniel set against Jesus
source_text: Εἶθ᾿ ἑξῆς ὡσπερεὶ σκοπὸν ἔχων τὸ συμπληροῦν βιβλίον ἐβούλετο ἡμᾶς μᾶλλον τὸν Ἰωνᾶν νομίσαι θεὸν ἤπερ Ἰησοῦν, Ἰωνᾶν, τὸν κηρύξαντα μετάνοιαν μιᾷ πόλει τῇ Νινευὴ, προκρίνων Ἰησοῦ, τοῦ κηρύξαντος μετάνοιαν ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ καὶ μᾶλλον ἐκείνου ἀνύσαντος. καὶ τὸν μὲν „ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ τοῦ κήτους“ τεραστίως ποιήσαντα καὶ παραδόξως „τρεῖς ἡμέρας καὶ τρεῖς νύκτας“ ἐβούλετο ἡμᾶς ἀναγορεῦσαι θεὸν, τὸν δ᾿ ἀναδεξάμενον ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων ἀποθανεῖν οὐκ ἤθελε Κέλσος, μαρτυρούμενον ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ διὰ τῶν προφητῶν, ἄξιον εἶναι τῆς δευτερευούσης μετὰ τὸν θεὸν τῶν ὅλων, δι᾿ ἃ ἐποίησεν ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς ἀνδραγαθήματα, τιμῆς. καὶ Ἰωνᾶς μὲν, ἵνα ·μὴ κηρύξῃ τὸ προστεταγμένον ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, κατεπόθη ὑπὸ τοῦ κήτους, Ἰησοῦς δὲ, ἐπεὶ ἐδίδαξεν ἅπερ ὁ θεὸς ἐβούλετο, τὸν ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων θάνατον ἀνεδέξατο. ἑξῆς δέ φησιν ὅτι ἔδει μᾶλλον τὸν Δανιὴλ, ἀναβάντα ἀπὸ τῶν λεόντων, προσκυνεῖσθαι ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν ἤπερ τὸν Ἰησοῦν. τὴν ἀγριότητα πάσης δυνάμεως ἀντικειμένης καταπατήσαντα καὶ ἡμῖν δόντα „ἐξουσίαν πατεῖν ἐπάνω ὄφεων καὶ σκορπίων καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ ἐχθροῦ“. εἶτα μὴ ἔχων ἄλλους λέγειν φησίν· ἢ οἱ τῶνδε ἔτι τερατωδέστεροι, ἅμα ἵνα λοιδορήσῃ τὸν Ἰωνᾶν καὶ τὸν Δανιήλ· τὸ γὰρ ἐν Κέλσῳ πνεῦμα εὐλογεῖν δικαίους οὐκ ἠπίστατο.
pass_a_gloss: Then next, as if (ὡσπερεί) having as aim (σκοπός) to fill up (συμπληρόω) a book, he wanted (βούλομαι) us rather to consider (νομίζω) Jonah god than Jesus, Jonah, the one having preached (κηρύσσω) repentance (μετάνοια) to one city, Nineveh, preferring (προκρίνω) him to Jesus, the one having preached repentance to the whole world (κόσμος) and having accomplished (ἀνύω) more than that one. And the one who 'in the belly (κοιλία) of the sea monster (κῆτος)' prodigiously (τεραστίως) and marvellously (παραδόξως) spent (ποιέω) 'three days and three nights' he wanted us to proclaim god, but the one having undertaken (ἀναδέχομαι) to die on behalf of men, witnessed (μαρτυρέω) by God through the prophets, Celsus was not willing (ἐθέλω) to be worthy of the honour (τιμή) second (δευτερεύω) after the God of the wholes (τῶν ὅλων), on account of the brave deeds (ἀνδραγαθήματα) he did in heaven and on earth. And Jonah, so that he might not preach what was commanded (προστάσσω) by God, was swallowed down (καταπίνω) by the sea monster, but Jesus, since he taught what God wished, undertook the death on behalf of men. Next he says that Daniel, having come up (ἀναβαίνω) from the lions (λέοντες), ought rather to be worshipped (προσκυνέω) by us than Jesus, the one having trampled (καταπατέω) the savagery (ἀγριότης) of every opposing (ἀντίκειμαι) power (δύναμις) and having given us 'authority (ἐξουσία) to tread (πατέω) upon serpents (ὄφεις) and scorpions (σκορπίοι) and upon all the power of the enemy (ἐχθρός)'. Then not having others to name he says: 'or those still more portentous (τερατώδης) than these', at the same time so that he may revile (λοιδορέω) Jonah and Daniel; for the spirit in Celsus did not know how (ἐπίσταμαι) to bless/speak well of (εὐλογέω) righteous men (δίκαιοι).
pass_b_english: Then, next, as if his aim were to fill up a book, he wanted us to think Jonah a god rather than Jesus, preferring Jonah, who preached repentance to one city, Nineveh (Jonah 3:4–5), to Jesus, who preached repentance to the whole world and achieved more than Jonah did. He wanted us to proclaim as a god the man who, by a prodigy and against all expectation, spent “three days and three nights” “in the belly of the sea monster” (Jonah 1:17; Matthew 12:40); but the One who undertook to die for mankind, to whom God bore witness through the prophets, Celsus would not allow to be worthy of the honour that ranks second after the God of the universe, for the mighty deeds he did in heaven and on earth. And Jonah, so as not to preach what God had commanded, was swallowed by the sea monster (Jonah 1:3, 17), whereas Jesus, because he taught what God willed, took upon himself death for mankind.

Next he says that we ought to worship Daniel, who came up from the lions (Daniel 6:23), rather than Jesus, who trampled down the savagery of every opposing power and gave us “authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19). Then, having no others to name, he says, “or others still more fantastic than these”, so as to revile Jonah and Daniel at the same time; for the spirit in Celsus did not know how to speak well of the righteous.

choices.choice: Origen paraphrases Celsus’s taunt from 7.53; only the closing phrase ἢ οἱ τῶνδε ἔτι τερατωδέστεροι is Celsus’s exact wording and is set in quotation marks (‘more fantastic’, as in 7.53). The three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster: Septuagint Jonah 2:1 = English Jonah 1:17; Origen’s words ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ τοῦ κήτους τρεῖς ἡμέρας καὶ τρεῖς νύκτας match both Jonah 2:1 LXX and Matthew 12:40. ‘Achieved more than Jonah did’ (μᾶλλον ἐκείνου ἀνύσαντος) may echo Matthew 12:41 (‘something greater than Jonah is here’), but not clearly, so it is not cited inline. ἵνα μὴ κηρύξῃ is kept as a purpose clause (‘so as not to preach’): Jonah’s flight to avoid preaching led to his being swallowed (Jonah 1:3, 17). ‘The honour second after the God of the universe’ (τῆς δευτερευούσης μετὰ τὸν θεὸν τῶν ὅλων ... τιμῆς) is kept exactly; Origen elsewhere speaks of the Son as second after the Father. ‘Daniel, who came up from the lions’ is Origen’s restatement of Celsus’s ‘Daniel from the beasts’; Daniel 6:23 in English numbering. The staged full stop before τὴν ἀγριότητα is read as a comma, since καταπατήσαντα and δόντα go with τὸν Ἰησοῦν. Luke 10:19 is quoted exactly. εὐλογεῖν rendered ‘speak well of’. The interpunct in ἵνα ·μή is a transcription artifact. Review: Daniel 6:23 is the English numbering (Greek and Aramaic 6:24); the earlier note that the numbering is the same was wrong. ‘commanded him’ trimmed to ‘commanded’, as in the Greek.
'the honour second after' -> 'the honour that ranks second after'
ἀνεδέξατο: 'accepted' -> 'took upon himself' (same verb as ἀναδεξάμενον, 'undertook')

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
